item.title: Hegseth Calls for Sweeping Military Education Changes in Naval War College Address
item.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced sweeping education directives supporting his effort to de-civilianize military higher education and align it with warfighting priorities on Monday at the Naval War College. A total of 33 directives were unveiled on Monday. Among key changes were an AI-aided capstone wargame in lieu of a written thesis for graduates and expanded access to classified information for course instruction. To facilitate greater use of classified information in the study of war, Hegseth said he was ordering accelerated capital investments to build and expand sensitive compartmented information facilities or SCIFs, at every war college campus to clear

item.title: Royal Navy Commissions First Unmanned Surface Vehicle Squadron
item.description: The Royal Navy commissioned its first unmanned surface vessel squadron last week as it transforms into a hybrid fleet, the service announced Monday. The 1st Autonomous Squadron was formally commissioned in a ceremony on Thursday at His Majesty’s Naval Base, in Portsmouth, England, according to a news release. The unit is the Royal Navy’s first ever autonomous squadron. “That makes this a genuinely historic occasion. For generations, the fleet has been built around ships, submarines and aircraft, manned by sailors and Royal Marines. From today, an autonomous squadron takes its place alongside them,” Royal Navy Fleet Commander Vice Adm. Steve

item.title: Obituaries for November 8
item.description:
Jason “Aba” Kaleo‘okalani Abadilla, 48, of Hilo, died Oct. 6 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. He was born in Hilo and was a fence installation supervisor with the federal government, was also an avid fisherman, diver and a member of the 100-plus ulua club. Visitation 10-11 a.m. Saturday (Nov. 14) at New Hope-Hilo Church. Memorial service at 11 a.m. Casual attire; no flowers. Survived by wife, Keala “Ala” Abadilla of Hilo; sons, Keson Abadilla, Kade Abadilla, Kaleo Abadilla and Kekoa Abadilla of Hilo; daughter, Kawehi Abadilla of Hilo; brother, Joey (Lana) Abadilla Sr. of Hilo; sister, Annie (Cody) Alvarez of Keaau; sisters-in-law, Kaycie (Ryland) Uchima and Laura (Jerome) Harada of Hilo, Kimberly DeMotta of Pepeekeo; a granddaughter; aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for November 8 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: The Future of French Fleet Close-in Defense
item.description: TOULON, France — Behind the bridge wings of one of Europe’s most modern combat supply ships, a team of French sailors donned gloves and flash hoods. The group were preparing for a close-in defense drill aboard Bâtiment ravitailleur de forces-class (BRF) resupply ship FS Jacques Stosskopf (A726) last month. At its Toulon naval base berthing, the modern logistics vessel was flanked by the anti-aircraft and anti-submarine escorts of France’s sole carrier strike group. Its size is considerable compared to previous generations of French combat support ships, one of which was rusting away at a pier to Jacques Stosskopf’s portside. Jacques

item.title: III MEF Extends Curfew for Junior Members in Okinawa Following Murder Indictment
item.description: The U.S. military extended a curfew on Okinawa for junior service members that was scheduled to expire on Sunday and is continuing to impose restrictions on the purchase and consumption of alcohol. The curfew for grades E-1 through E-4 was extended for 30 days and restricts them to their personal housing from 12 a.m. to 5 a.m., according to a Thursday news release from the III Marine Expeditionary Force (MEF). The curfew was previously in place for higher grade personnel but was lifted. However, all personnel are prohibited from the purchase or consumption of alcohol outside of their primary residence

item.title: Pacific Horizons School receives donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Pacific Horizons School (PHS) is pleased to announce receiving a generous $20,000 donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation in support of the PHS 2nd Annual Giving Campaign. This contribution represents a significant investment in the school’s mission to provide high-quality educational opportunities for students in American Samoa.

The PHS Annual Giving Campaign was launched in 2025 to help secure the school’s long-term future amid changes to federal Consolidated Grant funding. This grant offset approximately 15% of the school’s operating costs. With restrictions now in place, PHS faces a deficit that poses challenges to maintaining its programs. 

The Giving Campaign invites community partners to serve as “Anchor Donors,” aligning with the school’s nautical theme, by helping PHS reach its $70,000 goal. This support will directly strengthen the school’s general fund and ensure continued access to high-quality, well-rounded education for future generations.

Pacific Horizons School extends its warmest thanks to the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation for its partnership and philanthropy. Their support helps make it possible for PHS to continue building a strong, innovative, and student-centered future.

For more information about the PHS Annual Giving Campaign or ways to support, please contact Veronica Soto, School Director at veronicasoto@pacific-horizons-school.com (684) 699-5787.

item.title: Obituaries for November 6
item.description:
John “Curly” Castillo, 87, of Hilo died Aug. 24 at a private care home. Born in Papaaloa, he was a retired senior warehouseman for The Gas Company, member of New Hope Hilo, Community of Christ, Hui Okinawa, former member of ballroom dance clubs and U.S. Marine Corps veteran. Visitation 9-10:30 a.m. Friday, Nov. 13, at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Celebration of life at 10:30 a.m. Inurnment to follow at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2. Casual attire. Survived by wife, Ruth Y. Castillo of Hilo; stepchildren, Jennifer (Kevin) Nakano of Keaau, Gaven (Shelley) Fukunaga and Grant (Alise) Fukunaga of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Katherine (Keith) Higa of Hilo and Barbara (Charles) Bostwick of Molokai; brothers-in-law, Michael (Laurel) Matsuda of Waimea, Richard Weiser Jr. of Hilo, Dan (Jonnie) Weisgerber and Leon (Kristi) Weiser of Waimea, Franklin (Wendy) Weiser of Waikoloa; caregivers, Romeo and Helen Sembran of Hilo; 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for November 6 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Marines Identify Member Who Died After Fast-rope Training in Japan
item.description: Lance Cpl. Devin Hernandez died this week after he was injured during fast-rope training in Japan, the 3rd Marine Division announced Thursday. Hernandez, 25, sustained injuries during training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa. He was transported for medical treatment and later died from his injuries. “The Marines and sailors of 3rd Marine Division mourn the loss of one of our own. We extend our deepest condolences to Lance Cpl. Hernandez’s family, friends and fellow Marines,” said Maj. Gen. Kyle Ellison, commanding general of 3rd Marine Division, in a news release. The incident remains under investigation. Hernandez was a Maryland native.

item.title: USS Stout Loses Power During Port Visit Due to ‘Engineering Casualty’
item.description: A deployed destroyer recently lost power during a port visit to Italy, USNI News understands. USS Stout (DDG-55) was in port in Augusta Bay, Italy, for a scheduled port visit on Oct. 25 when it experienced an engineering casualty, causing the ship to lose power, Cmdr. Lauren Spaziano, U.S. 6th Fleet spokesperson, told USNI News. The Navy restored power for critical systems within 36 hours, with full power restored within three days. “While the U.S. Navy conducted repairs, the crew had continuous access to food, water and alternate lodging. To maintain operations security, we do not comment on ship schedules

item.title: Defense Primer on U.S. Special Operations Forces
item.description: The following is the Nov. 3, 2026, Congressional Research Service report Defense Primer: U.S. Special Operations Forces. From the Report U.S. Special Operations Forces (SOF) are active duty and reserve components of the military services that are designated as SOF by the Secretary of Defense, who is using “Secretary of War” as a “secondary title” under Executive Order (EO) 14347, dated September 5, 2025. SOF are selected, organized, trained, and equipped to conduct and support special operations. Special operations frequently require unique modes of employment, tactics, techniques, procedures, and equipment. SOF often conduct special operations in hostile, politically, and/or diplomatically

item.title: TBS ATM machine now available at the airport
item.description:
Source: PAAS press release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Port Administration American Samoa (PAAS) has announced the opening of a Territorial Bank of American Samoa (TBAS) Automated Teller Machine (ATM) at Pago Pago International Airport, providing travelers, airport employees, and the general public with convenient access to banking services. 

PAAS considers the new ATM as another positive step in Port Admin's ongoing efforts to improve airport facilities, enhance customer convenience, and deliver a better overall experience for residents and visitors traveling through American Samoa's primary international gateway.

Port Director Barney Sene expressed his appreciation to TBAS Chief Executive Officer Owen Peery and his team for recognizing the public need and working collaboratively with Port Administration to make this service available. 

“We sincerely thank TBAS CEO Owen Peery and his entire team for recognizing this important public need and responding with a practical solution,” he said.

“Improving the airport experience is not just about major infrastructure investments. It is also about providing the everyday services and conveniences that make travel easier for our residents and visitors.”

Sene added, “Our goal is to make Pago Pago International Airport more welcoming, convenient, and responsive to the needs of the people we serve. We appreciate TBAS stepping forward as a partner in that effort and look forward to continued collaboration.”

Local News
Tags: 
ATM MACHINES

item.title: ASCC Ethnomusicology Forum showcases SOLFA string ensemble
item.description:
“From Kitara to Orchestra: Mapping the String Traditions of Samoa”
By 
James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA  — The Fine Arts Department at the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) hosted its 5th annual Ethnomusicology Forum on Wednesday, October 28th. Intended to stimulate student interest, the forum typically explores some aspect of Music studies particularly relevant to the field. 

The theme of this year’s forum was “From Kitara to Orchestra: Mapping the String Traditions of Samoa”, and the discussion traced the evolution of SOLFA, a string ensemble and music education group based in the Independent State of Samoa that seeks to integrate a western classical music approach with Samoan musical traditions. 

To help set the stage for the event, on the day before the forum three members of SOLFA performed a late afternoon mini-concert for the ASCC students and staff.

Featured performers included Rosaivitilesaualofaoleola “Rosa” Solomona, co-founder and president of Solfa, on vocals and violin; Rosa’s brother Philton Solomona on violin and saxophone; and Haydon Afele-Nickel on violin. 

The three musicians gave ensemble as well as solo performances, with a repertoire ranging from classical pieces to Samoan melodies, showcasing how easily music from different cultural contexts can co-exist within a single performance. 

While only three of its musicians participated in the mini-concert and forum at ASCC, SOLFA regularly collaborates with many other players and singers in Samoa and beyond, and is equally adept at performing in either a small or a large-sized configuration.

At the forum itself, to give a broad overview of the history of western string instruments in relation to the music of Samoa, the forum presentation was divided into segments, the first of which was “Migration & Adaptation: The Arrival of the Strings”.

This section highlighted the arrival of the guitar and ukulele in Samoa via sailors, traders and missionaries, beginning a long integration process with the culture of Samoa. Keynote speaker Susau Konousi Solomona (mother of Rosa and Philton), Lecturer of Music & Performing Arts in the Faculty of Education at the National University of Samoa, shared insights based on many years of study, including anecdotes of the limited introduction of violins to Samoa by missionaries in the 1800s.

Next, the focus of the forum shifted to the present day for “The Genesis, Legacy and Politics of SOLFA”, for which Rosa Solomona served as guest speaker and recounted the formation and early activities of the string ensemble. Envisioning a group that could combine western music education with local cultural interests, Solomona found that bringing those two worlds together often required political negotiations, regional representation, and community support. Nevertheless, Solomona managed to work through the challenges, and in only a few years SOLFA established itself as a credible artistic and cultural entity.

The final portions of the forum consisted of a question-and-answer exchange, followed by a musical finale in which the SOLFA musicians collaborated with the ASCC Vocal Ensemble. 

ASCC Fine Arts Department chairperson Mr. Kuki Tuiasosopo subsequently deemed the forum a success and thanked all of those who participated. “Fa’afetai tele lava colleagues,” said Tuiasosopo, “community members, and especially our students who joined us on Tuesday evening’s free concert and yesterday’s Ethnomusicology Forum!  Thank you for your support of our efforts.”  

Tuiasosopo also credited local collaborators for their role in organizing SOLFA’s visit to American Samoa. 

“We are deeply grateful for the wonderful partnership and collaboration with the Arts Council Executive Director Ammon Fepulea’i, Music Coordinator John Mailo, and Program Director Magdalene Leauanae of DOE Division of Curriculum and Instructions,” he said. “Together, we share a vision to preserve, perpetuate, and strengthen our Samoan musical heritage for the future generation. 

“Bringing SOLFA on campus has reignited an interest among our students in Samoan instrumental music.  Therefore, we are committed to revive our instrumental ensembles, and working alongside the arts council and DCI, the future looks brighter for MUS 170 Beginning Orchestra, and MUS 180 Band.”

For more information on SOLFA, visit their pages on Facebook or Instagram, or their web page at: https://solfamusic.org
 
           

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
OLFA string ensemble

item.title: Zoning Board rejects CTC variance application
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — For the second time in just over a year, local construction company Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) has been denied permission by the American Samoa Zoning Board to establish its retail and production operations at a new location.

The latest rejection came after the board voted to deny CTC's zoning variance application for a site in Tula, where the company had proposed relocating its operations after failing to secure approval for an earlier proposal in Leone.

CTC's planned operation included the retail sale, hauling, and storage of cinders, sand, rock aggregates, and other construction materials. The company also sought approval for laboratory testing of construction materials, rental of heavy equipment, truck and heavy machinery maintenance and repair services, and the manufacture of concrete and construction products.

With its administrative offices located in Pava'ia'i, CTC operated for more than a decade from its former production and retail headquarters in Fogagogo near Maliu Mai Beach Resort.

However, that chapter came to an end in 2025 when the company's lease expired and was not renewed.

After losing its Fogagogo location, CTC sought alternative sites from which to continue its operations. Company officials reportedly applied for space at the government-owned Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park in Tafuna but were informed that no suitable lots were available.

The only government-owned property available at the time was a tract of land in Vailoa, Leone, commonly known as the "Airstrip."

CTC subsequently sought zoning approval to operate from the Airstrip property, but the proposal generated widespread opposition from nearby residents.

The site is surrounded by residential neighborhoods and is located near Leone High School, Leone Midkiff Elementary School, the Western District Health Center, the Leone Police Substation, and numerous family homes.

Residents packed public hearings before the Zoning Board, voicing concerns about dust, noise, heavy truck traffic, environmental impacts, and potential health risks. Written objections were also submitted to board members.

The strong community opposition ultimately played a significant role in the Zoning Board's decision to deny the Leone application in August of last year.

Undeterred by that setback, CTC returned to the Zoning Board last month seeking approval for a new site in Tula.

The proposed location sits on communal land belonging to the extended family of company owner Tony Togia'i.

Appearing on behalf of her husband, who was off-island at the time, Mrs. Togia'i told board members that the family had granted permission and fully supported the company's plans to establish a brick-manufacturing operation on the property.

She said CTC had gone to considerable lengths to gain community support before submitting its application.

According to Mrs. Togia'i, the company met with families living near the proposed site and received their approval. She submitted a petition bearing the signatures of those who supported the project.

She also informed the board that CTC had already invested substantial sums in specialized equipment, including a brick-manufacturing machine, and had constructed a purpose-built building designed to contain noise produced by the operation.

Mrs. Togia'i emphasized that brick production would only occur during designated daytime hours to minimize disturbance to neighboring residents.

Toward the end of last month, Zoning Board members Jim McGuire and Fofoga Sagato conducted a site inspection of the proposed Tula facility.

During their visit, they observed that there appeared to be no residences immediately adjacent to the operation.

Company owner Tony Togia'i accompanied the board members and explained the scope of the project. He also indicated that only one neighboring resident remained opposed to the operation.

The following day, McGuire visited that resident, Falaula Silivelio Vaoesea Aofia, to hear firsthand the concerns that had prompted his objection.

In an interview witnessed by Samoa News, Aofia described a very different picture of life next to the proposed CTC operation.

The retired U.S. Army veteran said construction activities on the site began approximately two years ago and involved extensive excavation work, heavy machinery activity, and large-scale earthmoving operations.

According to Aofia, the work has significantly affected the quality of life for his family.

"The breeze that comes from the ocean side of the village blows directly toward our home," Aofia explained. "When they operate the heavy machinery, the cement mixers, and the brick-making equipment, the noise is loud and the wind carries large amounts of dust toward our house."

He said the situation has become particularly difficult because of existing health conditions affecting both him and his wife.

"The air we breathe has become unsafe," he said. "It aggravates respiratory problems and prevents us from opening our windows or spending time outside."

Aofia noted that his wife is wheelchair-bound and suffers from respiratory ailments that could be worsened by dust generated by the operation.

He added that he also faces numerous health challenges and receives full medical benefits through the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

Aofia stated that he suffers from Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) resulting from his military service and said the constant noise from heavy equipment can trigger anxiety and stress.

The retired veteran also expressed frustration about how information regarding the project was communicated to residents.

Aofia said he believed he should have been informed much earlier about the proposal before it reached the Zoning Board.

He specifically questioned why the village pulenu'u had not made greater efforts to notify residents about a project that could directly affect their lives.

His frustration intensified when he reviewed the petition submitted by CTC in support of the application.

According to Aofia, he recognized many of the names on the document, including the signature of the village pulenu'u, who is also his first cousin.

Another signature that drew his attention belonged to a neighbor employed by the Department of Health.

Aofia said he had previously asked the individual to report what he viewed as health concerns associated with the operation to appropriate authorities.

Visibly upset, Aofia questioned how so many people who were familiar with his family's concerns had nevertheless signed the petition supporting the project.

Last Friday, as the Zoning Board met in executive session to make final decisions on pending variance applications, Aofia made an unexpected appearance.

To the surprise of several board members, he personally delivered a formal written complaint detailing his objections to the CTC operation.

Aofia explained that he had learned of the meeting through board members who had visited the site and felt compelled to ensure that his concerns were placed on the record before a final decision was made.

After considering the matter, board members voted to deny CTC's zoning variance application.

The decision marks the second unsuccessful attempt by the company to secure a new location for its operations following the loss of its longtime Fogagogo site, leaving the future location of one of the Territory's largest construction-material suppliers uncertain.

item.title: ASCC hosts Congressional Forum
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — With voters set to head to the polls tomorrow for the midterm elections, four of the five candidates seeking American Samoa's seat in the U.S. Congress took part in the American Samoa Community College Congressional Forum held on campus last Friday.

The four candidates that participated were Sandra King-Young, Tuifagaloa Dr. Afu Lefaoseu III, Meleagi Suitonu Chapman, and incumbent Uifa'atali Aumua Amata Radewagen. The fifth candidate, Fualaau Rosie Tago Lancaster did not attend the forum.

During the forum, candidates were asked to address a range of issues affecting the territory, including the status of several construction projects at ASCC that have been stalled for nearly two years. Concerned about the lengthy delays and their impact on students, faculty, and the college's future growth, moderators asked the candidates what role their office could play in identifying the obstacles that have prevented the projects from moving forward.

Specifically, the candidates were asked what steps they would take, if elected, to work with federal agencies, local officials, and other stakeholders to determine the causes of the delays, remove any barriers to progress, and help secure the support needed to restart and complete the long-awaited projects.

SANDRA KING-YOUNG

Responding to the question, Sandra King-Young said that a member of Congress could help address issues related to the federal funding supporting the stalled projects by engaging directly with the relevant federal agencies and exercising congressional oversight.

She explained that one of the key responsibilities of a member of Congress is to communicate with the agencies providing the funding and determine whether any issues or obstacles are preventing the projects from moving forward. This would involve meeting with agency officials, gathering information, and working to identify solutions in collaboration with the college and the community.

However, King-Young emphasized that once federal funds are allocated and transferred to the American Samoa Government, responsibility for administering and implementing those funds rests with ASG.

"As a member of Congress, we have to be careful we don't overstep that jurisdiction," King-Young said.

She reiterated that while the execution of federally funded projects falls under ASG's authority, the territory's congressional representative can still play an important role by maintaining communication with the funding agencies, monitoring the status of the projects, and helping bring stakeholders together to determine what steps are necessary to remove obstacles and ensure the projects move forward toward completion.

According to King-Young, a collaborative approach involving the federal funding agency, the college administration, the community, and the territorial government would be essential to getting the long-delayed construction projects back on track.

TUIFAGALOA DR. AFU LEFAOSEU III

Responding to the same question, congressional candidate Tuifagaloa Dr. Afu Lefaoseu III said that if elected, one of his top priorities would be working closely with the Governor's Office and American Samoa Community College (ASCC) officials to determine what is needed to move long-delayed campus improvement projects forward.

Tuifagaloa said he would first seek a comprehensive assessment of the college's infrastructure needs and identify projects that are ready for funding and construction.

"The first thing I would do is bring a congressional delegation here, people who are directly involved in funding and approving major capital projects," Tuifagaloa said. "Just by looking around the college, it's obvious that a great deal of work needs to be done. Not only do existing facilities require renovation and modernization, but there is also a growing need for new buildings to accommodate the steady increase in student enrollment each year."

He said he would aggressively pursue Capital Improvement Project (CIP) funding through federal agencies such as the U.S. Department of the Interior's Office of Insular Affairs and the U.S. Department of Education, while also seeking matching funds and other financial support to accelerate construction efforts.

According to Tuifagaloa, securing adequate funding will require a coordinated approach involving both federal and local partners. He added that he would also work on legislation affecting ASCC to ensure that critical infrastructure projects receive the attention and resources they deserve.

"We really need funding to turn these projects from plans into reality," Tuifagaloa said. "I will work hard to promote and advocate for funding opportunities, whether they come from federal programs, local government sources, or other available grants. Improving the college's infrastructure should be a priority because many of the facilities urgently need repair, upgrading, and modernization. Our students deserve a campus environment that supports their education and prepares them for the future."

The congressional hopeful emphasized that investing in ASCC is an investment in the territory's future workforce, noting that modern classrooms, laboratories, and student facilities are essential to meeting the educational demands of a growing student population.

MELEAGI SUITONU CHAPMAN

Congressional candidate Meleagi Suitonu Chapman was the next to address the issue, expressing strong support for strengthening educational opportunities for the younger generations of American Samoa and ensuring that students have access to quality learning environments and resources.

Chapman said that if elected to Congress, she would make education one of her top priorities, with a particular focus on improving academic achievement and supporting the long-term development of the ASCC.

She emphasized the importance of maintaining ASCC's accredited status, noting that accreditation is critical to ensuring students can continue to access quality higher education programs, transfer opportunities, and federal educational assistance.

She emphasized that education is an investment for the future and everything must be done to help students succeed academically while also ensuring that ASCC remains fully accredited and continues to meet the standards necessary to serve the community effectively.

Chapman added that she would advocate for federal resources and partnerships aimed at improving educational programs, expanding student support services, and addressing infrastructure and operational needs at the college.

She stressed that a strong and stable ASCC plays a vital role in preparing local students for careers, leadership roles, and further educational opportunities, while also contributing to the territory's economic and workforce development goals.

Chapman declared, "As your elected representative to Congress, I will continue to advocate for the college because its success is directly tied to the future of American Samoa."

Chapman emphasized that supporting ASCC goes beyond maintaining buildings and programs, describing it as an investment in the territory's next generation of leaders, skilled workers, and professionals.

"It's not about me, it's about you," she said. "It's about creating opportunities for our young people and ensuring they have access to a quality education right here at home. It is very important that our representative in Washington actively supports higher education and works to ensure American Samoa receives the recognition and resources it deserves."

She noted that there are areas where federal support and recognition could be strengthened and pledged to work closely with congressional leaders, federal agencies, and local stakeholders to address those concerns.

"If elected on November 3, I will make it a priority to advocate for ASCC and help secure the support needed to strengthen its programs, maintain its standing, and expand opportunities for our students," Chapman said. "Our future depends on the quality of education we provide today, and I will work tirelessly to make sure that future is a bright one."

Chapman concluded by reiterating that a strong educational system is essential to the territory's long-term economic and social development, adding that ensuring the continued success of ASCC would remain one of her key priorities in Congress.

UIFA'ATALI AUMUA AMATA RADEWAGEN

Incumbent Congresswoman Uifa'atali Aumua Amata Radewagen was the final candidate to address the issue. In her remarks, she highlighted federal funding efforts she has supported on behalf of American Samoa and emphasized that recent federal budget legislation did not reduce funding earmarked for the territory.

"The Big Beautiful Bill did not cut one red penny from American Samoa," Amata stated. "It cut a lot from the states, but it did not cut anything from American Samoa."

The congresswoman went on to explain that she successfully secured congressional designation of $3 million from a $6 million appropriation specifically for the ASCC. According to Amata, the funding is intended to support construction and infrastructure improvement projects on the ASCC campus.

She acknowledged that the allocation would not be sufficient to cover the costs of all of the college's planned capital improvement projects but said it represents an important first step toward addressing the institution's infrastructure needs.

"This may not pay for everything that needs to be done, but it's a start," Amata said. "The important thing is that the funding is there and available for the college to begin moving these projects forward."

Amata also urged ASCC officials to keep her office informed if any federally appropriated funds designated for the college fail to materialize or experience delays in the disbursement process.

"If money that has been appropriated by Congress for ASCC is not coming through, let me know," she said. "Once those funds are authorized and mandated by law, they are supposed to be delivered for their intended purpose. My office stands ready to follow up and make sure the college receives the funding that Congress has approved."

The veteran congresswoman reiterated her commitment to supporting ASCC's long-term growth, noting that investments in campus facilities, academic programs, and student services are vital to preparing future generations of American Samoans for higher education and workforce opportunities.

[![Congressional candidates at forum](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/img_7470.jpg?itok=KG9ZHHDH)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/img_7470.jpg?itok=JYMlkwxR)
By
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com
_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ With voters set to head to the polls tomorrow for the midterm elections, four of the five candidates seeking American Samoa's seat in the U.S. Congress took part in the American Samoa Community College Congressional Forum held on campus last Friday.
The four candidates that participated were Sandra King-Young, Tuifagaloa Dr. Afu Lefaoseu III, Meleagi Suitonu Chapman, and incumbent Uifa'atali Aumua Amata Radewagen. The fifth candidate, Fualaau Rosie Tago Lancaster did not attend the forum.
During the forum, candidates were asked to address a range of issues affecting the territory, including the status of several construction projects at ASCC that have been stalled for nearly two years. Concerned about the lengthy delays and their impact on students, faculty, and the college's future growth, moderators asked the candidates what role their office could play in identifying the obstacles that have prevented the projects from moving forward.
Specifically, the candidates were asked what steps they would take, if elected, to work with federal agencies, local officials, and other stakeholders to determine the causes of the delays, remove any barriers to progress, and help secure the support needed to restart and complete the long-awaited projects.
**SANDRA KING-YOUNG**
Responding to the question, Sandra King-Young said that a member of Congress could help address issues related to the federal funding supporting the stalled projects by engaging directly with the relevant federal agencies and exercising congressional oversight.
She explained that one of the key responsibilities of a member of Congress is to communicate with the agencies providing the funding and determine whether any issues or obstacles are preventing the projects from moving forward. This would involve meeting with agency officials, gathering information, and working to identify solutions in collaboration with the college and the community.
However, King-Young emphasized that once federal funds are allocated and transferred to the American Samoa Government, responsibility for administering and implementing those funds rests with ASG.
"As a member of Congress, we have to be careful we don't overstep that jurisdiction," King-Young said.
She reiterated that while the execution of federally funded projects falls under ASG's authority, the territory's congressional representative can still play an important role by maintaining communication with the funding agencies, monitoring the status of the projects, and helping bring stakeholders together to determine what steps are necessary to remove obstacles and ensure the projects move forward toward completion.
According to King-Young, a collaborative approach involving the federal funding agency, the college administration, the community, and the territorial government would be essential to getting the long-delayed construction projects back on track.
**TUIFAGALOA DR. AFU LEFAOSEU III**
Responding to the same question, congressional candidate Tuifagaloa Dr. Afu Lefaoseu III said that if elected, one of his top priorities would be working closely with the Governor's Office and American Samoa Community College (ASCC) officials to determine what is needed to move long-delayed campus improvement projects forward.
Tuifagaloa said he would first seek a comprehensive assessment of the college's infrastructure needs and identify projects that are ready for funding and construction.
"The first thing I would do is bring a congressional delegation here, people who are directly involved in funding and approving major capital projects," Tuifagaloa said. "Just by looking around the college, it's obvious that a great deal of work needs to be done. Not only do existing facilities require renovation and modernization, but there is also a growing need for new buildings to accommodate the steady increase in student enrollment each year."

According to Tuifagaloa, securing adequate funding will require a coordinated approach involving both federal and local partners. He added that he would also work on legislation affecting ASCC to ensure that critical infrastructure projects receive the attention and resources they deserve.
"We really need funding to turn these projects from plans into reality," Tuifagaloa said. "I will work hard to promote and advocate for funding opportunities, whether they come from federal programs, local government sources, or other available grants. Improving the college's infrastructure should be a priority because many of the facilities urgently need repair, upgrading, and modernization. item.title: Enterprise Hulk Towed from Newport News Shipbuilding
item.description: The hulk of former nuclear aircraft carrier USS Enterprise (CVN-65) was towed from a pier at Newport News Shipbuilding on Monday, almost 15 years after its final deployment, USNI News has learned. “Ex-Enterprise began its final transit this morning, departing Newport News Shipbuilding for Mobile, Alabama, where the ship will be dismantled,” reads a Monday statement from PAE Maritime. The remnant “Big E” is now in route to Mobile, Ala., after a court battle between environmental disposal contractor NorthStar and HII over which company would oversee the final disposal. Last month, HII dropped a legal challenge on the Navy’s decision

item.description: Marine Rotational Force-Southeast Asia is now on its second continuous rotation to the Philippines, the service announced last week. MRF-SEA held a rotation turnover on Oct. 26. item.title: Beyond Religion: The Difference Between What We Preach and How We Live
item.description:

item.title: Residents of Happy Valley voice their opposition to proposed shopping center
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Residents of Happy Valley are speaking out against a proposal by local company O&O Enterprises to build a shopping center behind Veterans Memorial Stadium in Tafuna, warning that the development could dramatically worsen traffic conditions, disrupt the character of their neighborhood, and pose serious safety risks to children and families living in the area.

The proposed project would be constructed on a four-acre parcel of land located behind the stadium and adjacent to the narrow one-lane road that links the neighboring communities of Petesa and Happy Valley. Both areas are already heavily populated residential neighborhoods where residents say traffic congestion is a daily challenge.

The development has been a subject of controversy since O&O Enterprises first submitted its land-use permit application to the American Samoa Zoning Board in January 2025. Over the past two years, the application has been repeatedly reviewed, postponed, and scrutinized before eventually being denied by the Board earlier this year.

One of the primary reasons cited for the denial was concern over the project's potential impact on nearby residential communities. Board members concluded that a shopping center of that size would likely generate a substantial increase in vehicle traffic through Petesa and Happy Valley, transforming what are now residential streets into busy commercial access routes.

They also expressed concern that the increase in traffic would place additional pressure on existing infrastructure, create safety hazards for residents, and diminish the quiet residential character that has long defined both neighborhoods.

In an effort to address those concerns, O&O Enterprises General Manager Sefulu Fuimaono told the Zoning Board during last week's reconsideration hearing that the company is prepared to fund several public improvements if the project receives approval.

The proposed improvements include widening portions of the access road, adding an additional traffic lane, constructing pedestrian sidewalks, and installing a bus stop near the shopping center.

Despite those concessions, several Board members remained unconvinced, maintaining that the proposed improvements would not eliminate the fundamental problem of directing large volumes of commercial traffic through residential areas.

The hearing concluded without a final decision. Vice Chairman Motuiliu Vesi Matu'u announced that the application would be taken under legal advisement, allowing Board members additional time to evaluate the testimony and review issues involving traffic access, zoning requirements, and the overall impact of the project on surrounding communities.

While the Board deliberates, residents say their opposition remains unwavering.

Several Happy Valley residents contacted Samoa News yesterday to express their concerns, arguing that the proposed shopping center would fundamentally alter life in the neighborhood.

They said traffic along the Petesa-Happy Valley corridor is already difficult to navigate during peak hours and warned that the addition of hundreds of customer vehicles each day would only make conditions worse.

Parents in particular voiced concern about the safety of children who regularly walk, bicycle, or play near the roadway.

"If the shopping center is approved, there will be vehicles moving through here all day," one resident said. "We're worried about our children being able to safely cross the road or even walk through the neighborhood."

Others argued that the development would bring increased noise, air pollution, and congestion to an area that was never designed to accommodate a major commercial complex.

Several members of the Jehovah's Witnesses congregation, whose Kingdom Hall is located directly opposite the site of the proposed shopping center along the narrow one-lane road, also voiced strong opposition to the development. They told Samoa News that the increased traffic, noise, and activity generated by a large commercial complex would be disruptive to worship services and other church activities.

Congregation members said the area is currently relatively peaceful and that the construction of a shopping center across the road would fundamentally change the atmosphere of the neighborhood. They expressed particular concern about the constant flow of vehicles, delivery trucks, and customers expected to use the road throughout the day and into the evening.

Among the residents opposed to the project is Failelei Paua'a, whose home is located at the end of the one-lane road.

Paua'a told Samoa News that he was unaware of the proposed development until Zoning Board members James McGuire and Fofoga Sagato visited the area and sought his views during a site inspection.

"If it wasn't for the Board members coming here and asking me about the project, I would never have known anything about it until construction started," he said.

Paua'a said he is particularly concerned about how the development would affect access to his property.

"If this project is given the green light, there would be a lot of traffic right in front of my driveway," he explained. "I would have a hard time entering and exiting my property, especially during peak shopping hours."

He noted that traffic congestion is already a problem along the one-lane road, even without a major commercial development at the end of it.

"Right now, I already have to deal with vehicles stopping in front of my gate while drivers wait for cars coming into Happy Valley from the Petesa side to clear the road before they can proceed towards Petesa," Paua'a said. "Adding hundreds more vehicles every day would only make the situation worse."

Residents also questioned why customer traffic could not be directed through an access road connected to Airport Road near the stadium rather than through residential neighborhoods.

Several echoed concerns previously raised by Zoning Board members that Airport Road is better equipped to handle the volume of traffic expected from a large commercial development and would minimize the impact on nearby homes.

Pastor Francis Vaivao Jr. of the Heart of Worship Assembly of God Church in Happy Valley also voiced strong opposition to the proposed development, warning that it would pose serious safety concerns for residents and create distractions for church members during worship services and other religious activities.

Speaking with Samoa News, Pastor Vaivao said he has witnessed firsthand the transformation of Happy Valley over the years and believes the community is already experiencing the effects of increased traffic.

"We were one of the first families to settle here," Pastor Vaivao recalled. "I miss the days when the only road into Happy Valley was a dirt road. Back then, there were very few vehicles passing by our home, and the area was much quieter."

He noted that conditions changed significantly after the one-lane road linking Happy Valley and Petesa was developed. According to Vaivao, many motorists traveling west now use the route as a shortcut, resulting in a steady flow of vehicles through what was once a quiet residential neighborhood.

"Traffic has already increased because drivers use this road as a shortcut," he said. "Now imagine what it would be like if a shopping center is built at the end of the road. The number of vehicles passing through here every day would increase dramatically."

Pastor Vaivao said the increased traffic would not only affect residents but would also disrupt church activities, as the church is located within the affected area.

He expressed concern that constant vehicle noise, congestion, and the movement of shoppers throughout the day would interfere with worship services, prayer meetings, youth programs, and other church gatherings.

Unlike some residents who have suggested that the project might be acceptable if access were provided directly from Airport Road, Pastor Vaivao said he remains firmly opposed to the development regardless of how vehicles enter the site.

He argued that a commercial project of this magnitude is simply incompatible with the residential nature of Happy Valley and the surrounding area.

"I am completely against the shopping center being built there," he said. "Whether the access road comes through Happy Valley, Petesa, or directly from Airport Road, I still believe the project is not the right fit for this community."

His remarks echoed concerns raised by other residents who fear the proposed development would permanently alter the character of the neighborhood and place additional pressure on roads and infrastructure that are already struggling to accommodate existing traffic.

According to them, the issue is not opposition to economic development itself but rather where and how that development takes place.

They say they support business growth and investment in the Territory, but believe it should not come at the expense of the safety, peace, and quality of life of families who have lived in Petesa and Happy Valley for generations.

With the Zoning Board's final decision still pending, residents are hoping their concerns will play a significant role in determining whether the project ultimately moves forward.

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ Residents of Happy Valley are speaking out against a proposal by local company O&O Enterprises to build a shopping center behind Veterans Memorial Stadium in Tafuna, warning that the development could dramatically worsen traffic conditions, disrupt the character of their neighborhood, and pose serious safety risks to children and families living in the area.
The proposed project would be constructed on a four-acre parcel of land located behind the stadium and adjacent to the narrow one-lane road that links the neighboring communities of Petesa and Happy Valley. Both areas are already heavily populated residential neighborhoods where residents say traffic congestion is a daily challenge.
The development has been a subject of controversy since O&O Enterprises first submitted its land-use permit application to the American Samoa Zoning Board in January 2025. Over the past two years, the application has been repeatedly reviewed, postponed, and scrutinized before eventually being denied by the Board earlier this year.
One of the primary reasons cited for the denial was concern over the project's potential impact on nearby residential communities. Board members concluded that a shopping center of that size would likely generate a substantial increase in vehicle traffic through Petesa and Happy Valley, transforming what are now residential streets into busy commercial access routes.
They also expressed concern that the increase in traffic would place additional pressure on existing infrastructure, create safety hazards for residents, and diminish the quiet residential character that has long defined both neighborhoods.
In an effort to address those concerns, O&O Enterprises General Manager Sefulu Fuimaono told the Zoning Board during last week's reconsideration hearing that the company is prepared to fund several public improvements if the project receives approval.
The proposed improvements include widening portions of the access road, adding an additional traffic lane, constructing pedestrian sidewalks, and installing a bus stop near the shopping center.
Despite those concessions, several Board members remained unconvinced, maintaining that the proposed improvements would not eliminate the fundamental problem of directing large volumes of commercial traffic through residential areas.
The hearing concluded without a final decision. Vice Chairman Motuiliu Vesi Matu'u announced that the application would be taken under legal advisement, allowing Board members additional time to evaluate the testimony and review issues involving traffic access, zoning requirements, and the overall impact of the project on surrounding communities.

item.title: U.S. Marine Drone Detachment in the Philippines Operating from Palawan Airfield
item.description: MANILA, Philippines — A U.S. Marine Corps drone detachment is operating from a Philippine airfield in Palawan near South China Sea flashpoints in the Spratly Islands, USNI News has learned. item.title: Final Farewell to American Samoa Meteorologist Leilua Mase Akapo
item.description:
Source: Facebook

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A final farewell to American Samoa Meteorologist Leilua Mase Akapo, longtime American Samoa meteorologist, a post he held for decades until his retirement. 

Leilua was the face of every major natural disaster including some of the most memorable Hurricane Ofa, Tusi and Val to tropical cyclones, floods and the devastating earthquake and tsunami of 2009. 

We all tuned in as he kept the public informed. 

He was both the trust and the calm of American Samoa during such times. Manuia lau malaga Mr. Akapo Akapo, as he was known to many of us. 

Heartfelt condolences to his children and family from the local community and Samoa News.

item.title: SKD Alpha Eta Chapter at ASCC holds Fall Induction
item.description:
By 
ASCC Staff
Source: ASCC

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Sigma Kappa Delta (SKD) is an English Honor Society for Two-Year Colleges nationwide. Founded in 1996 at Cottey College, the Sigma Kappa Delta Central Office is now located at Northern Illinois University. The Society strives to confer distinction for high achievement in English language and literature in undergraduate studies. Through its local chapters, SKD provides pro-cultural stimulation on college campuses and fosters all aspects of the discipline of English, including literature, language, and writing. The SKD expects its members to exhibit high standards of academic excellence; while serving society by fostering literacy.

The SKD inducts approximately 2,500 members annually at more than 100 active chapters across the country, with each chapter defined by its location and membership, yet bound to the rest by the common goal of promoting excellence in the disciplines of the English language. 

Every chapter has the opportunity to share its love of literature and linguistics with like-minded peers, participate in rewarding activities, and be recognized for their accomplishments. They may also apply for one or more of the Society’s numerous awards and scholarships.

A presence at the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) for six years now, on Thursday, October 15th, the Alpha Eta chapter of the SKD conducted its sixth induction ceremony. 

2026 Chapter President Oloitefumalevaipaepae Wilson led the ceremony, which took place in the ASCC Lecture Hall, assisted by officers Manufou Lotulelei (Vice President), Elshaddai Falesui (Secretary), Noel Tuitasi (Treasurer), Asifoa Lagai (Historian), and Lilien Ve’e (Marshal). The Alpha Eta Chapter welcomed eleven new members: J-La V. Afia; Elshaddai S. Falesui; Muluea T. Ilimaleota; Joslynn M. Lamese; Hazel I. Leo;Moesha S. Metuli; Ropina M. Salanoa; Kathy Sulusi; Aisali Vasai; Nalei A. Vaouli; and Lilien M. Ve’e.

As the Alpha Eta chapter celebrated its sixth membership installment, advisor Mrs. Ruta Tauiliili-Mahuka shared an exciting update on the rest of their fall 2026 activities. 

From its inception, the local SKD chapter began compiling and publishing volumes of local literature and artworks. Now, the group is releasing a new addition to their Pacific Voices series, titled Caught in a Constellation and Other Poems. 

Anyone interested in this book of original student creations is welcome to reach out to Alpha Eta president Wilson at o.wilson@amsamoa.edu for details. 

Every purchase helps fund Alpha Eta Chapter outreach programs. The society also intends to host two poetry and art workshops at local high schools, with an announcement to come on further details.

Anyone seeking further information on the ASCC chapter of the Sigma Kappa Delta, or who would like to inquire about their Pacific Voices publications, can also contact their advisor by email at r.tauiliili-mahuka@amsamoa.edu. 

Full details on the nationwide honor society can be found on its website at https://www.english2.org

A Class A mishap is defined by the Naval Safety Command as one that causes at least $2.5 million in damage and/or aircraft to be destroyed. item.title: Governor to launch anti-drug awareness campaign as public concerns grow over widespread drug abuse
item.description:
The problem can no longer be ignored, says territory’s leaders
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The launch of Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula's planned anti-drug awareness campaign next month comes at a critical time for American Samoa, as growing concerns mount over the spread of illegal drugs throughout the Territory. 

Over the past several years, community leaders, law enforcement officials, educators, church representatives, and families have increasingly voiced alarm over the widespread presence of crystal methamphetamine, commonly known as ice. Once considered a problem affecting only a limited segment of the population, drug abuse is now viewed as a crisis reaching into nearly every part of society.

Officials say the problem no longer affects only adults. Reports and community observations indicate that drug use is impacting people across multiple age groups, from middle-aged adults and young people, including high school students, to, in some cases, children of elementary school age. 

The growing reach of the drug has heightened concerns about its devastating effects on families, public safety, education, and the overall wellbeing of communities throughout the Territory.

Against this backdrop, Governor Pulaali'i's planned campaign is expected to place renewed public attention on the dangers of substance abuse while encouraging a united response involving government agencies, churches, families, schools, villages, and community organizations. Many believe the drug problem has reached an alarming level and requires a coordinated effort from every sector of society.

The issue came under the spotlight during the final Senate Standing Committee hearing of the 39th Legislature before lawmakers adjourned for their end-of-year recess. Members of the Senate Public Safety and Homeland Security Committee summoned officials from the Department of Public Safety (DPS), the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and Customs to explain their ongoing efforts to combat illegal drugs and strengthen border enforcement.

Chief Customs Officer Iuliano Falaniko told senators that Customs personnel detain individuals caught attempting to smuggle drugs through the Territory's ports of entry and immediately refer the cases to Homeland Security investigators. The same procedure applies to individuals who go to the Fagatogo Post Office to collect packages or parcels from off-island that are found to contain concealed narcotics.

Falaniko explained that in previous years such cases were referred directly to the DPS, which would then assume responsibility for detaining suspects and conducting investigations. However, a change in the law has shifted primary responsibility for handling these cases to the DHS.

"The process begins with a referral to the Attorney General," DHS Director Vaeotagaloa Glenn Lefiti explained. "Our responsibility is to conduct the investigation and provide a complete report of our findings. The Attorney General's Office reviews the facts, evaluates the evidence, and determines whether criminal charges are warranted."

The change became official after legislation approved by the Fono last year granted DHS authority to arrest and detain travelers attempting to bring illegal drugs into American Samoa through ports of entry, as well as individuals seeking to claim drug-laden packages arriving from off-island. Under the law, these investigations now fall under the jurisdiction of DHS.

Lefiti emphasized that while Homeland Security has been assigned responsibility for border interdiction and related investigations, DPS continues to focus on local drug enforcement operations within communities. He stressed that both agencies work closely together, along with Customs officials, in identifying, investigating, and apprehending offenders.

The DHS Director also highlighted the department's partnerships with federal agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), in efforts to protect American Samoa's borders from drug smuggling operations, human trafficking, and other transnational criminal activities.

Several senators, however, expressed concern about what they viewed as overlapping responsibilities between DHS and DPS.

Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono argued that the apparent duplication of duties could be undermining the effectiveness of anti-drug enforcement efforts. He pointed to figures contained in a report submitted by Lefiti indicating that only five drug-related cases had been recorded during 2025.

According to Togiola, that number appeared inconsistent with the numerous arrests reported by DPS during a series of drug raids, as well as the quantities of methamphetamine seized in those operations.

"This doesn't add up," Togiola remarked, questioning whether different agencies were using separate reporting systems that failed to present a complete picture of the Territory's drug problem.

Another issue raised by senators was the growing threat of fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid that has fueled a deadly overdose crisis in many parts of the United States.

At the close of the hearing, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean asked whether Homeland Security, Public Safety, and Customs were adequately prepared to prevent fentanyl from entering American Samoa and to respond should it gain a foothold in the Territory.

Lefiti's response was blunt.

"No," the Homeland Security Director admitted.

He told lawmakers that American Samoa currently lacks the resources, specialized equipment, and training necessary to effectively address the unique dangers posed by fentanyl. He said DHS is actively pursuing federal grant funding to strengthen detection capabilities and provide advanced training for personnel.

The concerns raised at the hearing highlight the urgency behind Governor Pulaali'i's upcoming anti-drug awareness campaign.

Speaking at a recent press conference, the Governor stressed that defeating the Territory's drug problem will require more than law enforcement efforts alone. He called on families, churches, schools, village leaders, and community organizations to become active partners in the fight against illegal drugs.

He warned that the growing drug epidemic is tearing families apart, contributing to crime, and placing the future of many young people at risk.

"This has become a very serious problem," Pulaali'i said. "We must come together as a community to address it before more lives are lost and more families are harmed."

The campaign, which is scheduled to begin in early November, will be spearheaded by the newly established eight-member Opioid and Substance Abuse Council (OSAC) operating under the Governor's Drug Control Office.

The council has been tasked with coordinating public education campaigns, prevention initiatives, and substance abuse programs throughout the Territory. It will also serve as the government's primary advisory and oversight body for opioid-related and substance abuse initiatives, ensuring compliance with the Opioid Settlement Agreement and its approved abatement strategies.

Members of the council include Assistant Attorney General Louise Lafitaga, Acting Commissioner of Public Safety Lauti Tautalasoo Moliga, Department of Health psychiatrist Dr. Peni Biukoto, Homeland Security Director Vaeotagaloa Glenn Lefiti, Deputy Treasurer Levi Reese, clinical psychologist Dr. Jueta Eta McCutchan, faith-based community advocate Rev. Iasepi Ulu, and victims advocate Ipu Lefiti of the Pae ma le Auli Organization.

The Governor emphasized that while government agencies have a responsibility to enforce the law and provide resources, lasting success will depend on the willingness of the entire community to become involved.

"The government cannot address this alone," he said. "Our families, churches, schools, and villages all have a role in protecting our people and helping prevent drug use in our communities."

As American Samoa prepares for the launch of the campaign, many hope it will mark the beginning of a broader Territory-wide effort to confront a problem that residents, church leaders, lawmakers, and law enforcement officials alike say can no longer be ignored.

BACGROUND

In the meantime, the territory is currently awaiting a new facility that is being built for the comprehensive care for individuals receiving behavioral health, mental health, and substance abuse rehabilitation services — the American Samoa Department of Health’s new Behavioral Health & Drug and Alcohol Rehabilitation Clinic. 

The governor has commended the collaborative efforts of the Department of Health, the ARPA Oversight Office, and all partners involved in moving this project forward. The facility is being built by Silva Group Corporation.

item.title: Marine Rotational Force Concludes Deployment to the Outback
item.description: Marine Rotational Force-Darwin 26.3 completed its six month rotational deployment to Australia and the Indo-Pacific, the service announced on Friday. The conclusion of the MRF-D’s deployment marks the 15th rotation, reads a Marine Corps news release. During the deployment, the rotational force was certified as a Special Purpose Marine Air-Ground Task Force – the first time a MRF-D has received the special certification. The MRF-D, led by 5th Marine Regiment, 1st Marine Division, combined 2,000 Marines and sailors from I and III Marine Expeditionary forces into a force capable of bringing together command and control, aviation, ground combat and logistics

item.title: Let’s Talk Food: How to make a good Neapolitan pizza
item.description:
The poor classes of Naples, many living in the ghettos, were the first to eat pizza in the 18th century. The crust was flatbread, and the sauce was made with tomatoes brought from Peru, and the explorers who brought them thought they were poisonous. The wives of the fishermen often made them and called them “pizza marinara.”

The post Let’s Talk Food: How to make a good Neapolitan pizza appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Completion of new Airport Terminal parking lot expansion targeted for June 2027
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMMOA — The Port Administration of American Samoa (PAAS) has provided an update on the development of the Airport Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project at the Pago Pago International Airport (PPG). The critical infrastructure project is moving forward steadily with overall completion of 35%, and target completion date of June 30, 2027, according to the media release.

PAAS Director Barney Sene said, “The Airport Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project represents an important investment in the future of the Pago Pago International Airport and the infrastructure needed to support the new Airport Terminal Facility construction. Although much of the current work is taking place underground and may not be readily visible to the public, these improvements to the drainage, sanitary, power, and utility systems are essential components of the overall new airport terminal project. We are pleased with the progress being made and appreciate the continued efforts of our contractor and utility partners.” 

The Director added, “We understand that construction activities can create temporary challenges for our airport users and the community. We greatly appreciate the patience, cooperation, and understanding of our travelers, visitors, and residents as this important work continues. Our priority remains completing the project safely and efficiently while maintaining continuous airport operations.”

Contractor Paramount Builders, Inc. has maintained an active pace of work despite recent rainy weather. Construction activities are currently focused on vital underground drainage and utility infrastructure to support the future new Airport Terminal Facility. Recent progress includes: 

Construction activities are currently focused on underground drainage and utility infrastructure to support the future new Airport Terminal Facility. [Photo: PIOA/ Woolpert]

DRAINAGE AND STRUCTURES:
Completion of cast-in-place concrete culverts, structure base pours, and formwork, including the pouring of storm structures and protective concrete covers.

SANITARY SUSTEMS: 
Successful installation of 160 linear feet of 12-inch sanitary piping on the north side of the site, alongside necessary density testing.

UTILITY MODERNAZATION: 
Close coordination with local utility providers to manage underground power connections, safely navigate junction box placements, and install utility poles to support temporary telecommunications cables to the airport terminal.

To maintain an active and safe construction zone while ensuring continuous airport operations, a public traffic setup has been established at the main parking lot entrance and exit. This requires a temporary road rerouting, complete with specialized striping patterns, directional signs, and safety barricades.

PAAS acknowledges that navigating construction zones can be challenging and extends its formal appreciation to the public, airport travelers, visitors, and the wider community for their continued patience, cooperation, and understanding as we build a more modern, secure, and optimal facility to serve American Samoa.

The Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project is an important step toward providing a more modern, secure, efficient, and functional airport facility to better serve the people of American Samoa and visitors to the territory.

item.title: Samoa's forgotten fagufagu makes a comeback
item.description:
Source: Samoa Observer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A traditional Samoan musical instrument that disappeared from the country's soundscape more than a century ago is making a comeback, with efforts underway to restore the knowledge of how it was made and played.

The fagufagu, or nose flute in English, once used in traditional music, poetry and ceremonial practices, is being reintroduced through workshops and performances involving Samoan and other Pacific practitioners.

Tanuvasa Tau’ili’ili Alpha Maiava, co-director of Talanoa Arts Forum, is among those 

According to Tanuvasa, the fagufagu began disappearing from Samoa's traditional soundscape during the 1800s, with Christianity, colonisation and Western musical influences contributing to its decline.

Over time, the knowledge of how to construct and play the instrument was also lost as fewer people passed these skills on.

With limited documentation available in Samoa, those involved in the revival have turned to other Pacific countries where similar traditions have survived.

Tanuvasa has worked with Tongan master instrumentalist Tu’ifonualava Kaivelata and the Hikule’ao o Ono’aho collective, known in Samoan as Si’uleo o Anamua.

Tongan practitioner Saia Tuitahi also visited Samoa to demonstrate construction techniques to Galumalemana Steven Percival at the Tiapapata Arts Centre.

In February 2026, workshops were held at five locations across Samoa as part of the Samoa Arts Fono, introducing participants to the fagufagu and other traditional sound practices.

Tanuvasa said the instrument was beginning to appear more frequently in performances, although much of its traditional knowledge remained to be recovered.

“While the instrument is now appearing more frequently in performances, much of the deeper knowledge surrounding its construction, cultivation, and traditional use is only now beginning to be reclaimed,” he said.

The revival aims to ensure future generations can not only play the fagufagu but also understand its place in Samoan culture.

Local News
Tags: 
nose flute

item.title: Obituaries for October 25
item.description:
Vernon “Jr. Boy” Ai, 73, of Hilo died Oct. 2 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Hilo, he was a retired warehouse supervisor for Veterans Produce Exchange, maintenance worker for Kings Shop Waikoloa and former member of Hilo Jaycees and Classic Car Cruisers. Visitation 9-10 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 31 at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Funeral service at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at Homelani Memorial Park, Ilima Section. Casual attire. Survived by wife, Sandra Ai of Hilo; daughters, Sherry (Jared Miyake) Ai, Nell (Jay) Costa and Sheryl (Randall) Yoneda of Hilo; sister, Verna Duarte of Oahu; sisters-in-law, Drue Ai of Kailua-Kona and Joy Ai of Oahu; 10 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for October 25 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Güzelyurt: Turkey’s ‘beautiful land’
item.description:
Güzelyurt, a town on the edge of Turkey’s rural region of Cappadocia, is one of my favorite discoveries in this bizarre and fascinating corner of central Turkey. It sits at the edge of the Ihlara Valley, about 35 miles from the regional capital of NevSehir. It’s best known in Turkey as a town where historic enemies — Greeks, Turks, Kurds, and Bulgarians — live in peace. I like it as a place with almost no tourism, lots of history, and plenty of Turkish character.

The post Güzelyurt: Turkey’s ‘beautiful land’ appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Former intern in Amata’s local office talks about her time as a Peace Corps Volunteer
item.description:
Source: Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s D.C. staff

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is congratulating Peace Corps Volunteer Rosalina Macon, a former intern in the congressional office, and currently featured in an article on the Peace Corps website. She is from Manu’a and the villages of Utumea, Fagaalu, and Vailoa.

In her studies at North Carolina A&T State University, Rosalina twice had the opportunity to study abroad. Those in turn inspired her desire to reconnect deeply with her Samoan heritage, increase fluency in the Samoan language, and consider the Peace Corps with the idea of possibly serving in Samoa. Instead, she was offered the opportunity for a new experience staying in the Indo-Pacific region and serving in Indonesia, the world’s largest archipelagic nation of islands. It is the world’s fourth-most populous country, and in the top 15 in the world by total land area.

In Indonesia, after three months of focused training, then moving there on her birthday, she began teaching English while working on her use of the local language, Sundanese. She quickly established friendships and a special support network with three local English teachers she now calls her “sisters,” as well as finding a welcoming community from the locals.

Along with her teaching assignment at Islamic Middle School in Java, the world’s most populous island, she and the teachers there are implementing fun vocabulary words, strengthening students’ opportunities through an English club outside the structure of the classroom, and planning for an English camp. 

Rosalina said, “It has been a privilege to serve as a Peace Corps volunteer in Indonesia. I’ve been blessed to work alongside my Indonesian counterparts and community to create projects together, and along the way I’ve learned so much about Indonesian culture while getting to share my own in return. Not every day is easy, but I’m constantly reminded that I represent more than myself. I carry my family and my communities in American Samoa and South Carolina with me, and I’m proud to represent them. Though service isn’t a foreign concept to me, this experience has simply been a continuation of that lifelong commitment.”

“Congratulations to Rosalina, who worked as an intern in our office in Tutuila. She has a bright future through her intelligence, assertiveness, and deep interest in influencing policy for the betterment of people’s lives,” said Congresswoman Amata. “She’s putting those interests to great use right now with the Peace Corps, which will lead to more open doors. I know her family and friends in American Samoa and South Carolina are following this phase of her life closely, and we are proud of her in American Samoa!”

Congresswoman Amata serves as Co-Chairman of the bipartisan Peace Corps Caucus in the U.S. House of Representatives, with Congressman John Garamendi (D-CA). They have worked for reauthorization legislation and emphasized the expansion of the Peace Corps back into more nations following pandemic recovery, including the Indo-Pacific region.

item.title: Obituaries for October 23
item.description:
Jeffry Lynn Brinkley, 74, of Waikoloa died Sept. 18 at home. Born in Texas City, Texas, he had a doctorate in nursing practice, served in the U.S. Army and retired from the U.S. Public Health Service as a captain, then taught at the University of Hawaii School of Nursing. Services with military honors held. Survived by wife, Marcia Brinkley of Waikoloa; daughters, Carolyn (Santiago) Pena of Spring, Texas, Elizabeth (Earl) Smith of Tyler, Texas, and Shannon Brinkley of Hingham, Mass.; brother, Steve (Belaine) Brinkley; brothers-in-law, Gerald (Janet) Scheider, David (Beverly) Scheider and Robert Scheider; four grandchildren and a great-grandson; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for October 23 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.
